prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement of time

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest case on the shortlist of a new measurement technique that changes what can be observed. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the conflict between tight confinement and ultranarrow-transition spectroscopy, so a very large number of neutral atoms can be interrogated in the Lamb-Dicke regime with Doppler and recoil shifts suppressed and quantum projection noise reduced. Ye's group then turned this into the demonstrated record in systematic uncertainty (near 1e-18) and into direct clock-to-clock comparisons, including gravitational redshift across millimetre-to-centimetre height differences and many-body clock physics. This is a decisive coherence and linewidth-control story, backed by experiment rather than proposal. It has been independently reproduced at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST and elsewhere with mutual agreement at the 1e-18 level, and it feeds relativistic geodesy, fundamental-constant and dark-matter searches and the preparation for a redefinition of the second. A two-laureate attribution (invention plus realization at record performance) is compact and defensible, and it is distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and overlap. Others (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto, Hollberg, Diddams and the ion-clock groups) made decisive contributions, and the comb prize of 2005 (Hall, Hansch) and the 2012 Wineland prize cover enabling technology, so a lay reader may see this as a continuation of 'precision time' prizes. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the largest practical impact is still prospective. Finally, as the member with the strongest instinct for measurement science, I should discount my own bias toward metrology and test whether the committee would rank it first if the conceptual weight rather than the measurement precision were the criterion.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B014 first as a genuine conceptual step: magic-wavelength trapping combined with ultranarrow forbidden transitions controls projection noise and Doppler/recoil shifts together, with mutual agreement among many labs, and she ranks the Higgs experiments (B020) third as almost overdue.
responses.response: I agree with her on B014 and on the point that the Lamb-Dicke argument is what makes it an invention and not merely a better clock. Where I differ is B020: the discovery is plainly important, but the three-person limit forces a choice among Gianotti, Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee that I cannot defend on the evidence, whereas B014 has an attribution that maps cleanly onto invention (Katori) and realization at record performance (Ye). I would let B020 wait until the attribution question can be resolved rather than pick names for the sake of the prize being awarded.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics (B042) first as a tool that opens a door and ranks B014 second as an invention with measurable benefit, noting that Ruska 1986 is a precedent for recognising electron optics.
responses.response: I respect the tool-that-opens-doors argument, and it is close to my own criterion, so I take B042 seriously. My reservation is that the Rose/Haider/Urban trio covers the TEM corrector, while the STEM corrector (Krivanek) is a parallel, independently confirmed branch outside the credited names, so the attribution is weaker than for B014. I would also want to see evidence that B042 has enabled new physical discoveries rather than better images of known structures; for B014 the enabled measurements (redshift tests, constant drifts, dark-matter bounds) are already in the literature. I would keep it as a strong later candidate rather than this year's first choice.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube (B021) first as a discovery driven by nature rather than an elegant idea, with a secure diffuse flux and TXS 0506+056 and Galactic-plane evidence, but admits the allocation among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and AMANDA/DUMAND pioneers is delicate.
responses.response: I share his preference for results nature handed us, and I agree the diffuse flux is secure. But his own qualification is where I land: the flux is established while source identification rests on a few associations at modest significance, and the origin of the flux is largely open, so the astronomy is early. The credit among a large collaboration and precursors is also less clear than for B014. I would not exclude B021 and I would treat it as a serious future prize, but I would not yet rank it above a technique whose reproducibility is already at the 1e-18 level in several independent laboratories.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B009) first as the architecture of essentially all superconducting processors and the natural continuation of the 2025 prize, with B008 second and B014 third as low risk.
responses.response: I agree circuit QED is scientifically strong and independently confirmed across dozens of laboratories. My doubt is timing and differentiation from the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits: awarding a closely related circuit result one year later makes the committee's reasoning harder to defend, and the 'three-name cut' among Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Girvin, Devoret, Majer and Schuster is a judgement call you yourself describe. I do agree with you that B008 (Cirac, Zoller, Blatt) is a strong second, and I would like to hear whether you would support it as a fallback if B014 fails to carry the committee.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the Katori/Ye pair as sufficient or wants additional names (for example Lemonde, Ludlow, Hollberg) that would exceed the two-person configuration.
How much weight the unfinished redefinition of the second should carry; I think the demonstrated science is enough, but colleagues may want the redefinition decided first.
Whether B008 can be separated from the 2012 Wineland/Haroche prize cleanly, and whether choosing Blatt over Bloch splits the compound candidate unfairly.
Whether a second part combining B014 with a single-person B008 credit is workable; the three-person union limit makes it unattractive, so I propose a single-achievement prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B014. Minor notes: I am part of the WACQT leadership (superconducting-circuit oriented, overlapping institutionally with Johansson at Chalmers), which is relevant to B009, a candidate I have not ranked highly, so I would flag it if B009 moved forward. I have co-authored with European quantum-memory groups and have a general AMO/quantum-information background that overlaps with B008, but no named candidate there is a direct collaborator, mentor or Lund colleague.
